The Goal body ends with the run's constraints block, so a run and `hyp prompt` can find it:

```text
May change: <the repository, how it is changed (for example commits on one local branch, a PR never merged), and the texts the change makes wrong>
Read only: <repositories, directories or data the run may read but never change>
Never: <acts the run never takes, such as replacing an installed binary or publishing source data>
```

The block runs from the first line that starts with `May change:`, `Read only:` or `Never:` to the end of the body. It holds each of the three headings at least once, and every non-empty line in it starts with one of them, so write one constraint per line and put no other text after the block. A line of spaces, a tab or a lone carriage return is not empty: leave a blank line truly empty, and write the body with `\n` line ends. A heading may repeat, such as one `Never:` line per act. `hyp add goal` warns when a body has a heading but no valid block, and `hyp prompt` refuses that Goal.

A body that names another tree's ids writes each as `<tree>:<id>`. Then run `hyp status <G-id>` and `hyp check`: it must print `check: 0 errors`. Commit `.tree/events/` and `.tree/evidence/`.

## Hand off

hyp prints the `/goal` prompt for hyp-goal-run from the log. Choose a new runner actor, then run:

```text
hyp prompt <G-id> --actor <runner-actor> [--branch <branch>] [--pr <N>] [--experiments <N>]
```

It prints the store's path, the actor, the Goal id, the skill, the stop clauses (the runner owes nothing, or N Results under the actor, 5 by default) and the Goal body's constraints block, line for line; `--branch` and `--pr` add a clause each after the block. Give the owner its output as it is, and do not add to it. The prompt carries no owner answer: OWED lists each answer and each returned limit the runner applies. The practice of a run, a build Goal's review round included, is in hyp-goal-run. Run `hyp prompt` on the log the run starts from: the prompt names the Goal by its id, so the Goal's add must be in that log, merged or on the branch the prompt names. If `hyp prompt` refuses (exit 1), the Goal body has no valid constraints block; a Goal is never edited, so tell the owner, who adds a new Goal with a valid block. Exit 2 is a bad argument, such as a `--branch` with a space; exit 3 means no repository holds the store, so run it from the store inside its repository.

- Put a testable choice to the owner as a choice.
- Propose a stored field replay can derive.
- Write a line about history, process, an owner act or a reading.
- Add a purpose this Goal does not hold as a line; it is a new Goal.
- Write under the owner's actor without their approval of the exact command.
- End the grill with a question only the owner can answer still in chat and not in the tree.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# Issue #141: Run practice: the last candidate of a budget-bound run goes unreviewed
2	
3	Opened by dat9uy at 2026-11-12T02:21:06Z. Text as of 2026-11-12T03:45:00Z.
4	
5	## Event
6	
7	On 2026-11-12, run 1 of `investigations/goal-prompt` (G-ZBM2RE, PR #140) stopped with its last candidate, H-YXSJEM at `5c5902d`, never reviewed. The two earlier candidates were reviewed, and each review found real defects (10 findings on `10566d4`, 8 on `b4f23b2`). The stop checkpoint says "all review limits closed" and does not name the missing review.
8	
9	The chain, from the run's transcript and the two trees:
10	
11	1. A review finding that is a case of a line becomes a limit, and `--limit` exists only on `hyp record`. So the runner recorded each review as its own Experiment: E-C3GGGJ reviewed `10566d4` and E-7QQ2DP reviewed `b4f23b2`.
12	2. Each candidate therefore cost two Experiments, a gate and a review. The run spent E-HQWTA0, E-C3GGGJ, E-Z5BTZR, E-7QQ2DP and E-NZR3GV (the gate of `5c5902d`), and the stop clause "5 Experiments have been recorded" ended it.
13	3. The default of 5 was set from G-D1CH1R's runs, where every Experiment gates a commit and review findings went straight into fix commits (one Experiment per candidate; run 5 used 4).
14	4. At 17:21:37 the runner wrote "E5 is the last Experiment the budget allows, so this fix commit must close everything." `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` asks for "one review of each candidate commit's diff" before the stop. The prompt's stop clause and the skill conflict, and neither says which yields or that the gap is named at the stop.
15	
16	## Scope
17	
18	Core: the run practice of a Goal whose candidate is a commit (review, budget and stop report) in `hyp-goal-run`, and the stop clause `hyp prompt` prints. No self-review recipe is involved.
19	
20	## Rivals
21	
22	A tree holds this question; each option below is a rival Hypothesis, not a decision. The scenario that separates them: replay the G-ZBM2RE cut after R-8JQPWG (one Experiment left, a fix commit pending) and see whether the run stops with every candidate reviewed or with the gap named.
23	
24	- **H-one-experiment:** a candidate's review is part of its gate Experiment. One Result carries the test verdicts and the review's limits, so a candidate costs one Experiment again.
25	- **H-name-at-stop:** keep the practice; the stop checkpoint names each candidate without a review, so the gap is visible to the owner.
26	- **H-reserve-last:** when one Experiment remains, the runner reviews the current candidate instead of committing another fix, and stops with recorded limits.
27	- **H-raise-budget:** the default of `--experiments` rises (for example to 7) to fit a gate and a review per candidate.
28	
29	These can combine (H-name-at-stop with any other); the tree should say which hold alone.
30	
31	## Done means
32	
33	- A tree under this issue selects a rival, or a combination, from a run on the scenario above.
34	- After the change, a run that reaches its budget either has a review Result for its final candidate or names that candidate as unreviewed in the stop checkpoint.

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

---
name: hyp-goal-run
description: "Run a hyp tree under an owner's Goal and met rule as an unattended /goal, for a discovery Goal or a build Goal: act only on what OWED says the runner owes, test before asking, write readings the owner can answer, reassess the targets under the owner's answers, and stop with a report the owner can read from hyp status. Use when a /goal prompt names this skill, such as the one hyp prompt prints."
---

The `/goal` prompt names the tree, your actor, the Goal, the stop and the Goal body's constraints; `hyp prompt <goal-id> --actor <actor>` prints it from the log. This skill says how to work until that stop. Use it with the hyp-prototype skill, which says how to add Questions, Hypotheses, Experiments and Results, and the hyp-verification skill, which says how to run an Experiment.

## Start

- Read the Goal first with `hyp show <goal-id>`, including its checkpoints, because `hyp status` does not print its met rule.
- Everything you need is in the tree. Do not read session logs, reports or memory about earlier runs.
- The Goal's body states the run's constraints under three headings: `May change:` (what you may write, and how), `Read only:` (what you may read but never change) and `Never:` (acts you never take). Obey them. A `/goal` prompt may narrow them, never widen them. If a step needs something they forbid, refer it with a reason or record a reading, and stop.
- A store may hold many Goals. Then `hyp status` prints only a GOALS table and one Awaiting owner list, so run `hyp status <goal-id>` wherever this skill says `hyp status`: OWED, LINES, the stop line and the last checkpoint are per Goal. Name the Goal with `--goal <goal-id>` on `hyp checkpoint`.
- Print `hyp status` at the end of every turn.

## Work

Act on what OWED in `hyp status` says the runner owes, and on nothing else. Plan only the next Experiment.

- Use the Goal's must-fail cases as known-answer flaw cases, in the owner's terms.
- The recipe's checks may exist before the verdict rule, because `hyp add exp` pins them. Write and run no candidate until the rule is recorded on the Experiment.
- Try a new or changed check only on its cases' stand-ins, never on a candidate, until the rule is recorded. If a candidate shows a check is wrong anyway, do not just fix the check: write the case that shows it, in the Goal's terms with the outcome it must give, in a new version, and name that case in the Experiment body. A sentence that discloses a trial run pins nothing.
- `hyp record` and `hyp check` warn when a Result's text disagrees with its cited files: a verdict that a cited `verdict:` line contradicts, or a commit or hash in the observation or a limit that no cited file holds. Fix each one with a new Result that cites the file; a Result cannot change after it is recorded.

## Build Goals

A build Goal's candidate is a commit. Its practice:

- Each commit you test is one Hypothesis under the Goal's question, with the branch and the commit in its title. Tie its subject before the run with `hyp subject <H> --base <commit>`. A fix is a new commit and a new Hypothesis that supersedes the old one (`hyp supersede <new> --old <old>`).
- Write the tree with the installed hyp. Compile the candidate to a separate path, and never replace an installed binary.
- Pin the gate as a recipe when the repository keeps one, so a script decides the verdict. When none does, the Experiment on a commit uses `--recipe none --rubric reading`: its body states the gate as the rule, and the Result cites the gate's logs.
- Before you run anything, write each Experiment's verdict rule in its body: the Goal's lines it aims at, red on the base and green on the candidate for each new test, a removal check for each refusal (remove the refusal and show which test fails), and `go vet ./...` and `go test ./... -count=1`, or the repository's own gate. For skill text, run the original and the candidate skills on the same eval cases.
- Keep the logs under `.tree/evidence/<E-id>/` and cite them in the Result.
- Before the stop, ask a fresh subagent for one review of each candidate commit's diff against the design and the Goal's lines. Give it the code, the lines and the keys already settled, with the owner's words; do not give it your conclusion. Ask it to label each finding with the line it is a case of, or none.
- Sort each finding: a case of a line is a `--limit` you close or, only if void, refer; a question about a line's meaning is a reading; a defect in text you may edit is a fix commit; anything else is an out-of-Goal finding, named in the stop checkpoint, and it never holds the select.
- The run may push its branch and open or update one PR. It never merges.

## Before a trade-off

Before a Question goes to the owner as a trade-off, add one structure that is not among the candidates, and the cheapest variant of each contradicted rival that would hold. Run them through a new version of the pinned recipe and record the Result. If a new structure holds every check, say in a checkpoint that the rule does not decide this Question.

## Readings

- When a verdict rests on your reading of a Goal line, write the other reading as a strict check: a separate named command in the recipe, with its own known answers, that sets no verdict. Say so in the Experiment's verdict rule, and run it on the same candidates. Record the reading with `hyp record --reading`, naming the check and which candidates fail it. If the recipe cannot test the other reading, say that in the reading.
- When a verdict rests on the word of a reading that is still open under AWAITING OWNER, or on an owner answer another Result already reads, record the same reading on that Result too, word for word, with the same `--reading-of` key if it has one: a reading holds only its own Result's Question, and hyp prints identical readings as one question and warns when the owner answers only one. Record a copy only on a Result that judged a Hypothesis whose verdict differs from the strict check's outcome for it: a `supports` the check fails, or a `contradicts` the check passes. A Result whose judged Hypotheses the check gives the same outcome as the verdict gets no copy. The owner answers every copy in one answer, because `--answer` is repeatable.
- Before you record a reading, look for a test that can decide it. If a test fits the Goal's lines, write it, run it under the verdict rule, and record no reading. If a test needs a new Goal line, name the test, the fact it measures and the line in the reading, and ask the owner whether to run it. Ask the owner to choose a meaning only when no test can decide, and say why none can.
- Write each reading in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active verbs, one meaning for each word, and the Goal's words for things. Use this form:

  ```text
  <Goal line>: "<the words>" has two meanings. Meaning 1: <...>. Meaning 2: <...>. This run used meaning <n>. <Check> tests meaning <n>; <candidates> fail it. Question: <one question the owner can answer in their own words>?
  ```

  Give one small example of each meaning, in the Goal's terms. If the line does not have two meanings, state the case it does not clearly cover, then the question. A reading holds at most 600 characters.

## Owner answers

- When the owner answers a reading, record it with their exact words, `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and treat their answer as the meaning of that line. If the owner's words answer a reading but do not name it, ask which reading before you write; an answer must name its key. Do not leave a question only in chat.
- If the owner's answer itself has two meanings, record a reading of that answer with `hyp record --reading-of <R-id>#r<n>="<the form above>"`. It narrows the answer and never reopens it; the answer stays in force.
- Only the owner changes an answer. When they give new words for a reading they already answered, record them with the same `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their new words>"`; hyp derives that it is a revision. The earlier answer and the Results that applied it stay. Apply the new answer with a Result that `--applies` it, and test a successor (`hyp supersede`) of any Hypothesis the old answer contradicted.
- A limit the owner accepts is recorded with `hyp answer --accept "<key>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and a return with `--returns`. hyp admits an accept only of a limit you referred, and never under your actor.

## Reassess

Apply each answered reading that `hyp status` lists under OWED as `apply answer`, and act on each limit it lists.

1. For each answer, write one line: the owner's words, the check, and the candidates that fail it. If the owner is in this session, show the lines and wait for their yes. If not, write the lines in the Experiment's body.
2. For each Question, add one Experiment that names each answer it applies with `--aims`, and fix how its verdicts are decided before you run it: a rubric from `rubrics/` (`--rubric <name>@<version>`, a new rubric version when the answer changes the rule) or `--rubric reading` with the rule in its body. A recipe measures and never prints a verdict. To reassess records an earlier run kept, pin them with `--records .tree/evidence/<E-id>` and `--recipe none`. If an outcome is already known, say so in the rule. Give a verdict on every target, `inconclusive` when the run could not decide. Record its Result with `--applies` for each answer it applied. Old Results stay as they are.
3. If applying an answer raises a new question about what a Goal line or the owner's answer means, record it with `hyp record --reading` on that Result. A Result cannot change after it is recorded, so if it is already recorded, record a new Result under the same Experiment.
4. Act on each `limit` line under OWED, whichever Hypothesis its Result gave a verdict on: a limit is a case the Goal covers that no check ran. If a test within the Goal's lines can run the case on every candidate, add an Experiment with `--aims` at it, run it, and record `--closes` on the Result that ran the case. A close records that the case ran, whatever the verdicts: a candidate that fails the case is contradicted and the limit is still closed, so never write a rule that closes it only on a pass. A close covers every case the limit's text names; `hyp record` prints that text when it closes. Record each case you did not run as a new `--limit` on the closing Result, and refer that new key when its case is void or outside the Goal's lines. A claim that a case is void, out of scope or covered elsewhere is a limit and a refer, never a sentence in a body or an observation. When that claim rests on your reading of a Goal line, put the reading in the refer's text. Write one case per `--limit`. If no such test can, or the case is void for every candidate, refer it with your reason: `hyp checkpoint --refers "<key>=<why no test within the Goal can close it, or why the case is void>" --why "..."`; hyp refuses a refer with no reason. When the owner returns a referred limit, it is an ordinary `limit` line again.
5. End with the candidates left under each Question: none, one, or several, by alias.
6. Select only when OWED lists `select` for that Question: `hyp select <Q-id> <H-id> --why "..."`. Never confirm a select. Do not change the Goal or add new structures unless the owner asks.

## Goal lines

- The Goal's lines are limits keyed on the Goal, `G-<id>#<n>`; `hyp status` prints them under LINES. A Goal's lines come with its add and no later event adds one. If the Goal's body states lines and none is typed, they cannot be added to this Goal: tell the owner, who may add a new Goal with them (`hyp add goal … --line "<line>"`). Do not write them for the owner.
- A line is owed as a `limit` on each top-level Question with a candidate no closer covers. Run its case like any limit: aim at it with `--aims G-<id>#<n>`, and record `--closes G-<id>#<n>` on each Result that ran the case. A Result covers a candidate it gave a verdict on, or one whose whole subject (base, patch and files) one of the Result's cited runs holds, so tie each candidate before the run: `hyp subject <H> [PATH…] --base <commit> [--patch FILE]`.
- A line is never edited. What a line means is a reading. A line no test within the Goal can run is a refer, and the owner accepts or returns it. A new line or a new purpose is a new Goal, so a new tree: tell the owner, and do not write it.

## Stop


3. Then list every owner item with the exact command the owner runs: each item under AWAITING OWNER, each out-of-Goal finding (a new Goal or an issue), merging the PR, reinstalling hyp, and each personal skill that names a command the change altered.

usage: hyp <command> [flags]

Every write command needs --why and an actor (--actor or $HYP_ACTOR).
Statuses are derived from events; no command can set one.

setup:
  init                                   create .tree in the current directory
  version                                print the hyp version

write:
  add goal --title T [--body B] [--alias A] [--line L]... [--cite N=KEY]...
  add dq   --parent REF --title T [--body B] [--alias A]
  add hyp  --parent REF --title T [--body B] [--alias A] [--subject PATH]...
  add exp  --parent REF --title T --recipe NAME@V|none [--rubric NAME@V|reading] [--records PATH]... [--target REF|none]... [--alias A]
  record   --exp REF [--verdict REF=supports|contradicts|inconclusive]... --observation O [--evidence P]... [--limit L]... [--closes R#N]...
  retract REF | abandon REF | reaffirm REF
  supersede NEW --old OLD
  amend HYP --body B                     revise a Hypothesis body
  subject HYP [PATH...] [--base C]       tie a Hypothesis to the base and files that embody its claim
  link FROM depends_on|external_ref TO   unlink FROM TYPE TO
  select DQ [HYP]                        admitted only when hyp status owes it (no HYP: print the suggestion only)
  unselect DQ | defer DQ | withdraw DQ|EXP | resume DQ
  checkpoint [--summary S] [--goal G] [--refers K[=TEXT]]...   the runner's report: a summary, refers, or both
  answer [--answer R#rN=TEXT]... [--accept K=TEXT]... [--returns K=TEXT]...   the owner's act; no --why

read (REF/TIME: an event id, a node ref, or an RFC3339 time):
  status [--as-of REF|TIME] [--max-lines N] [--live]   orientation screen, 60 lines by default; --live hides contradicted rivals
  show REF|R-id#n|G-id#n [--as-of REF|TIME]  one node, or one limit or line, in full, with its history
  diff --since REF|TIME                       status changes and events since a point
  render --markdown [--as-of REF|TIME]        the whole tree as Markdown, untruncated
  check                                       rejected events, bad lines, warnings
  signals [--json]                            design marks for the whole tree: one-rival, D1
  events --json                               applied events in merge order, and rejected ones, as JSON for scripts
  prompt G-id --actor A [--branch B] [--pr N] [--experiments N]   the /goal prompt for a Goal, from its body's constraints block

bundle (a recipe in recipes/ or a rubric in rubrics/; a name lives in one library):
  bundle hash DIR [--json]               the bundle hash add exp --recipe or --rubric records for DIR
  bundle check                           every pin to a versioned bundle, in every tree under the repo root, still matches it
  bundle new NAME@1 [--rubric]           write a first recipe, or with --rubric a first rubric, beside the nearest .tree/ from hyp's template; fill every hyp:placeholder
  bundle new NAME@N --from NAME@M        copy bundle NAME@M to the next version NAME@N in its library, writing from:
27:_Avoid_: replay for re-running an agent session (that is an Experiment run with a session-replay recipe)
30:Everything replay derives from a store's events: each node, a derived record per node kind (Hypothesis, Question, Experiment and Result) with its own status word, the Goal's state, rejections, limits and selections ([spec §8](replay-spec.md#8-projection-what-replay-returns)). Nothing stores it; every read replays (ADR 0006). In code: `replay.Projection`.
46:A Goal whose candidate is a commit: building is a Goal like any other. A line asserts one property of the candidate, decided by its own tests or one pinned instrument: `[P]` pins what a valid input produces, and `[N]` pins that a forbidden state is refused. Each commit is a Hypothesis whose subject is the base plus that commit's change, and a fix is a new Hypothesis that supersedes it. Each Experiment's verdict rule asks for red on base and green on the candidate; the base of the red run's subject is where the build starts, and the Goal records no start commit. A finding of a run's review that is a case of a line is a limit; one that is not is an out-of-Goal finding. A change to a skill is a build Goal too (ADR 0021).
50:A node, `Q-`, under the Goal or a Hypothesis, that asks one design question; its children are rival Hypotheses, and any Experiment with no targets that informs the question. Its state is open, reopened, answered, deferred or withdrawn ([spec §7.4](replay-spec.md#74-designquestion-state)). Withdrawn here is a hold that `dq.resume` lifts; it is not an Experiment's close.
51:_Avoid_: issue, decision; withdrawn for an Experiment (see Experiment status)
57:A node, `H-`, under a DesignQuestion, that states one possible answer as a claim an Experiment can test. It may name its subject, what embodies the claim, tied with `hyp subject`: a base commit (`--base`), at most one patch over it (`--patch`), and files kept by each file's sha256, which over a base are its input files; two Hypotheses may share a subject, since the claim is what differs, and a Hypothesis with no subject, such as a diagnosis, is covered only when a Result judges it. Its status comes from the verdicts of non-retracted Results, or from a supersedes edge or an abandon ([spec §7.1](replay-spec.md#71-hypothesis-status-first-matching-rule-wins)); its subject changes no status.
69:A reading asks what the owner's words mean, and a trade-off asks which candidate to choose. Closing a reading changes no status, because statuses come only from verdicts. An answer that rules out a candidate takes effect when a later Result records `contradicts` on it. A closed reading is owed by the runner until a Result applies it (`hyp record --applies`, from an Experiment that aims at it), and the owner is not asked to choose on its question until then. An owner who changes an answer answers the reading again (`hyp answer --answer R-…#rN=TEXT`): the new words are the answer in force from then on, the earlier answer stays in history, and the reading is owed by the runner again until a later Result applies it. A revision changes no earlier event or verdict. One verb serves both: whether an answer is a first answer or a revision is derived from the reading's state.
73:The step after the owner answers a reading: an Experiment aims at the answered reading, and its Result applies the answer and gives new verdicts on its targets. The answer goes into a check of a new recipe version, or into the rule in the Experiment's body when its verdicts are decided by reading; either way the rule is fixed before the run. Earlier Results stay as they are. Closing a reading changes no status; a reassess does, through its verdicts. Until a Result applies the answer, `hyp status` lists it under Owed as `apply answer`.
80:Another Hypothesis under the same DesignQuestion. Two live rivals are **separated** when a non-retracted Result gives them different verdicts, and `hyp show Q` lists the pairs that are not; exhaustiveness is a property of the cases run on the candidates (see Limit), never of the set of rivals, which the owner may reserve. A live rival is live and not contradicted ([spec §7.1](replay-spec.md#71-hypothesis-status-first-matching-rule-wins)); the one-rival refusal and the one-rival and D1 signals read the live rivals of an Experiment's parent at its add ([spec §8](replay-spec.md#8-projection-what-replay-returns), Rivals at add).
83:**Experiment**:
34:- Before the stop, ask a fresh subagent for one review of each candidate commit's diff against the design and the Goal's lines. Give it the code, the lines and the keys already settled, with the owner's words; do not give it your conclusion. Ask it to label each finding with the line it is a case of, or none.

# Map: core and self-review

This repository holds hyp, and a few recipes and trees that test it. Records made before the public release stay in the private development history. This page says which concepts and files belong to which scope, so that an issue, a plan or a change can say which scope it serves. The two words are defined in [glossary.md](glossary.md), "Scopes of this repository".

## The test

Core and self-review are scopes. An item's scope is the concept it belongs to, not who uses it or what tested it.

- **Core** is every concept hyp has, and everything a user who installs hyp into another repository runs, loads or reads there. A user writes recipes, runs sandboxes and records trees for their own code, so recipe, sandbox, store cut, runner and instrument are core concepts, even where only self-review uses them today.
- **Self-review** is the recipes this repository keeps to test hyp, whatever repository the runner works on, plus the inputs only they use. Nothing else is self-review.

The repository a runner works on is its investigated repo, a core concept (spec §1). Here it was often hyp itself, and often a real outside project: session-replay's snapshots were sessions of a runner working on another application. Which repository it is does not change the scope.

Investigating hyp is an activity, not a scope. A tree takes its place by its question:

- A tree whose question is about hyp takes that question's scope. Most trees here ask whether a core concept works, so they are core-scope work, carried out with self-review recipes.
- A tree whose question is about another project is a self-review input: a run this repository keeps as evidence about hyp, not for its answer.

Three rules keep the boundary honest:

1. **A concept stays core when self-review is what tests it.** The runner was measured by session-replay, and it is still a core concept.
2. **A self-review recipe does not make its kind self-review.** session-replay was a recipe; recipes are core.
3. **Self-review invents no concept of its own.** Every word a self-review recipe uses maps onto core concepts (see "Self-review words" below). Work whose question is about a self-review recipe itself is a special case, and it needs a reason. Today there is one: an instrument must give its known answers before its verdicts count, which is a core rule applied to a self-review recipe.

There are exactly two scopes. An item that fits neither is a problem that has not been scoped well enough: split it until each part has one scope. `.agentkit/` is not an item of this project at all: it is the local development setup for working on the repository, like `.gitignore`.

## Visibility

Visibility is a separate axis from scope. Every item in this repository is public. A self-review row below marks its own visibility.

Round 1 is below. I've read the issue and its three comments, checked the code and checked the store. These facts shape the questions:

- **Store:** `investigations/goal-prompt` already holds #113's Goals (G-GZR6C6 and G-ZBM2RE), and #141 is "Part of #113". The new Goal goes in that store, so no `hyp init` is needed.
- **Cuts exist:** R-8JQPWG, R-3YJ7T2 and R-JHBCWS are all in the log. `hyp status --as-of` can show the tree at each.
- **Stale premise:** the issue says the sort rule is "in no skill on main". PR #140 has since merged, so it now sits in `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` line 34 and 35.
- **Test method:** no session-replay recipe is published, so "replay the cut" needs a different method (question 4).

**Please give me your actor name once**, for example `owner-dat`. I'll use it for the owner writes.

**1. How many Goals?**
- **Today:** #141 asks for two things. One is to select a practice from a run on the scenario. The other is a change so that "a run that reaches its budget has a reviewed final candidate or names the gap".
- **Problem:** the build Goal's lines (what `hyp prompt` prints, what the skill says) depend on which rival is selected. They cannot be written before the select.
- **Option A:** this Goal is a discovery Goal that selects the practice. Its candidate is a practice text plus a stop clause, tested on the scenario cuts. The build is a second Goal, which you add after the select.
- **Option B:** one build Goal now. Its candidates would be commits, and the rivals would have to be built before they are compared.
- **My recommendation:** A. Under B, a rival you reject would still have to be built first. The design record and its build were also two Goals for #113.

**2. Which questions does this Goal hold?** Each is a top-level DesignQuestion and every rival under it answers that question.
- **Q-review:** what happens to the last candidate when the budget runs out? The rivals are H-one-experiment, H-name-at-stop, H-reserve-last and H-raise-budget (default 7).
- **Q-passing-case:** what closes a case that the run's own probe passes on the candidate? The rivals are the current practice (a `--limit`, then a fix commit) and H-probe-closes (closed in the review's Result).
- **Q-review-scope:** what does a review read? The rivals are the latest increment (current) and H-whole-candidate (the cumulative diff from the base).
- **Why Q-passing-case and Q-review-scope belong here:** you raised both as causes of the same stop, and one scenario family covers them. Both run 2's and run 3's cuts end on an unreviewed or needlessly re-committed candidate.
- **Alternative:** each goes to its own Goal.
- **My recommendation:** keep all three here. The same lines apply to every candidate, and a rule that closes the gap under one question does not decide the other two.
- **Combinations:** the Goal body will say that H-name-at-stop must hold alone. A combination is added as a rival only if a single rival fails a case (the "add one structure" rule in `hyp-goal-run`).

**3. Lines.** These are cases every candidate must meet, and a check can run each one. My draft:
1. **[N]** A run stops on its budget with a candidate commit that has no review Result and is not named as unreviewed in the stop checkpoint. Applies to the cut after R-8JQPWG: one Experiment left, a fix commit pending.
2. **[P]** On run 2's cut after R-3YJ7T2 and run 3's cut after R-JHBCWS, where each review's findings are cases the run's own probe passes on the reviewed candidate, the run ends with its final candidate holding a review Result.
3. **[P]** The candidate's text states how a review is recorded (its own Experiment, or inside the gate's) and whether its Result counts against the budget.
4. **[N]** The stop clause `hyp prompt` prints and the skill's review rule disagree on the final candidate. The text says which yields when both cannot be met, and that the stop checkpoint names the gap.
- **Line 1 comes from:** your "Done means", and run 1's "all review limits closed", which hid the gap.
- **Line 3 comes from:** your comment that "no text says a review is its own Experiment".
- **Line 2 has no mechanism:** it states the outcome and never says "probe-closes". If it did, Q-passing-case would be decided by the line instead of by the run.

Do you approve or edit these four?

**4. Test method.**
- **Today:** the candidates are texts that a runner reads (the `hyp-goal-run` skill and the stop clause), tested on three cuts.
- **Option A:** use ak-skill-creator's eval flow, as G-ZBM2RE line 6 did. Each cut is a case and each candidate text is a run. The flow owns the cases, fixtures, matching and grading.
- **Option B:** build a new recipe for session replay.
- **My recommendation:** A.
- **Your preferences:** which model, how many trials per candidate and cut (I suggest 3), and what token or time budget?

**5. Not asked.**
- The 7 in H-raise-budget is only the example from the issue. It goes in the rival's body.
- Which rival wins is for the run to decide, not for you in chat.

Answer by number.

Actor name: owner-standin.

1. Agree: a new Goal in the existing `investigations/goal-prompt` store, since this is part of #113. I have no view on A vs B, so I accept your recommendation (A).

2. I want one question, not three. Put every candidate fix under a single question and test them all together. H-whole-candidate stays in as a rival, but I expect it to lose, because one cumulative review costs a lot. Treat it as the expected loser.

3. Before I approve the lines, say how each one serves two aims: a review must not easily run out of the run's budget, and a review must not go on and on because of small changes.

4. Use replayed runs on Sonnet, 3 trials per candidate and starting point. I don't want a full replay of a whole build from its start for every trial; it costs too much, so replay from the cuts only. Could the ak-context-engineering skill help with how to evaluate? Cost cap: a candidate may cost at most 1.5 times the base at the same starting point. How do you compute cost? A trial that hangs counts as the most expensive.

5. Agreed. The 7 goes in the rival's body, and the run decides the winner.

content.text:
Round 2 is below. The one blocker is question 4: `ak-context-engineering` is not installed here.

**Actor:** `owner-standin`.

**2. One question.** I'll put everything under one DesignQuestion: "What practice should a build run follow so its final candidate is reviewed within the budget, without review going on over small changes?"
- **Rivals:** H-one-experiment, H-name-at-stop, H-reserve-last, H-raise-budget, H-probe-closes and H-whole-candidate.
- **One cost of a single question:** each rival must be a complete practice. H-probe-closes and H-whole-candidate keep the current budget text and change one rule.
- **H-whole-candidate:** I'll record it as the owner's expected loser in its body. The run still gives its verdict from the cuts.
- **Combinations:** a combination is added as a rival only if a single rival fails a case.

**3. How each line serves your two aims.** Aim (a) is that a review must not easily run out of the budget. Aim (b) is that a review must not go on over small changes. My first draft covered (b) only weakly, so I've changed it.

| Line | Aim | How it serves it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 [N] stop with a candidate that has no review Result and is not named in the stop checkpoint (cut after R-8JQPWG) | (a) | A budget can run out, but not silently. |
| 2 [P] on run 2's cut after R-3YJ7T2 and run 3's cut after R-JHBCWS, where findings are only cases a probe passes, the run ends with its final candidate reviewed | (b) | Probe-passed cases are the small changes that chained reviews. |
| 3 [P] the text states how a review is recorded and whether it counts against the budget | (a) | The budget gets a stated unit. |
| 4 [N] the stop clause `hyp prompt` prints and the skill's review rule disagree on the final candidate | (a) | The text says which yields and that the checkpoint names the gap. |
| 5 [N] new: a candidate's mean cost at a cut is more than 1.5 times the base's mean at the same cut | (b) | This is your cap. A review chain that does not stop costs more. |

Line 5 names the base by sha256: `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` is `cb15e2f2…fa750e`, and the installed `hyp` is `c44fe92d…160c`. It asserts that the candidate differs from both.

**4. Test method.**
- **Replay from the cuts only.** Each trial starts from the store cut and the repository at that cut's commit, with a fresh Sonnet runner. It runs under the candidate text until it stops. The cuts are after R-8JQPWG, R-3YJ7T2 and R-JHBCWS.
- **Number of runs:** 7 practices (the base and 6 rivals) × 3 cuts × 3 trials is 63 runs.
- **`ak-context-engineering`:** it is not installed here. Only `ak-skill-creator` is under `.claude/skills` and `~/.claude/skills`. I won't guess its content. If you install it, the run can use it, but the Goal does not depend on it.
- **Cost, my proposal:** dollars per trial, from the trial's token usage at Sonnet prices. Input, output, cache write and cache read are priced separately. It sums the runner and every review subagent it starts, because the review is the thing being costed. I chose dollars over raw tokens because cache reads are cheap and raw tokens would overstate long contexts. A candidate's cost at a cut is the mean of its 3 trials. Line 5 compares that mean with the base's mean at the same cut.
- **A hung trial:** a trial is hung when it passes the wall-time or turn limit. Its cost is the highest cost of any trial at that cut, whichever practice it ran. If every trial there hangs, it is the cap.
- **What I need from you:** the limit. I suggest 60 minutes or 150 turns, whichever comes first. Is that right?

Please approve the five lines or edit them. After that I'll run the second reader, then show the routing table.

Read-only review. Repo: /Users/datguy/.hyp-sandbox/g146-pre-b-1/wt (hyp, a Go tool). Do not edit anything. Read AGENTS.md, docs/glossary.md (entries Goal, Limit, line, Experiment, Result, Rival, Subject), docs/replay-spec.md (select/OWED rules, line coverage), skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md and internal/cli/prompt.go.

An owner and a grill agreed this new discovery Goal, to be added to the existing store investigations/goal-prompt (which already holds Goals G-GZR6C6 and G-ZBM2RE):

Purpose: choose the review/budget/stop practice for a build Goal run (text of hyp-goal-run's review rule plus the stop clause `hyp prompt` prints), so that a run that reaches its budget has a review Result for its final candidate or names it unreviewed in the stop checkpoint, and review does not chain on small changes.
One DesignQuestion, six rival Hypotheses, each a whole practice (variant of skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md and prompt.go's stop clause): one-experiment (review inside the gate Experiment), name-at-stop, reserve-last (review the current candidate instead of another fix when one Experiment remains), raise-budget (default 7), probe-closes (a case the run's probe passes is closed in the review Result, not a limit), whole-candidate (review reads cumulative diff from base).
Method: each candidate is run by a fresh Sonnet runner started from a store cut (cuts: after Results R-8JQPWG, R-3YJ7T2, R-JHBCWS in investigations/goal-prompt) with the repo at that cut's commit, 3 trials per candidate per cut, hung trial = >60 min or >150 turns, cost = dollars per trial over runner plus review subagents, a hung trial costs the highest of any trial at that cut.
Lines (limits keyed on the Goal, owed on every candidate):
1 [N] A run stops on its budget with a candidate commit that has no review Result and is not named unreviewed in the stop checkpoint (cut after R-8JQPWG).
2 [P] On run 2's cut after R-3YJ7T2 and run 3's cut after R-JHBCWS, where each review's findings are only cases the run's own probe passes on the reviewed candidate, the run ends with its final candidate holding a review Result.
3 [P] The candidate's text states how a review is recorded and whether its Result counts against the budget.
4 [N] The stop clause hyp prints and the skill's review rule disagree on the final candidate: the text says which yields and that the stop checkpoint names the gap.
5 [N] A candidate's mean cost at a cut is more than 1.5 times the base's mean at the same cut; base = skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md sha256 cb15e2f2e207b5a66807c9369e4d776d5378e61c2dd99679c36dfba402fa750e plus installed hyp sha256 c44fe92d0c93a4e2d4e1797df9dfd567f0233f67b00494c441acfa6881dc160c, and the candidate differs from it.
The build of the selected practice is a later, separate Goal.

Walk each line through scenarios the grill did not draw: (a) two Goals in one store, the new one and G-ZBM2RE, both with candidates, and hyp status/OWED/line coverage/hyp prompt for the new Goal; (b) a merged log from two actors; (c) the base moving mid-run (main or the skill file changing); (d) a candidate that changes both skill text and prompt.go, and a rival that is only a prompt flag value (raise-budget); (e) a trial run whose cut contains the Goal itself, so the candidate could read or edit the tree it is judged by; (f) a line that cannot be decided on some candidate or cut (line 1 on the other two cuts, line 2 on the first cut, line 5 on the base itself, line 4 for a rival that changes no text of the stop clause). Report concrete defects only: which line or rule, the input, the wrong outcome, with file:line evidence. Say plainly if a scenario holds. Under 500 words.
